## Background

Where do bees go in the winter? And how do they survive?

[![Bombus impatiens, the common eastern bumblebee. Photographed in New
Jersey. By Mousebelt - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0,
https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=98700493](BumbleBee.jpg){fig-alt="Picture of bee (Bombus impatiens) on flower"}](https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=98700493)

New common eastern bumblee (*Bombus impatiens*) queens (gynes) nest
underground after mating in the fall. They start new colonies the
following spring. Given that, how do they survive rain and snow during
their hibernation, which may last for months?

A lab accident led to the discovery that bees may be able to survive
submersion [@hibernat].

## 1

During an experiment focused on the impact of insecticides on common
eastern bumblebees, a graduate student was keeping bee queens in
soil-filled tubes in the refrigerator (to mimic winter conditions). One
day she noticed some of the tubes were filled with water. She quickly
removed the bees but expected them to be dead. Instead, 20 out of 21
were still moving.

This may be an example of where statistics is not needed. Why?

## 4

Note during creation: understand the data

```{r}
bee_data <- read.csv("data_flooding.csv", stringsAsFactors = T)
```

```{r}
summary(bee_data)
unique(bee_data$Bee_ID)
```

143 unique bees

```{r}
library(Rmisc)
summarySE(bee_data, groupvars = c("Bee_ID"), measurevar = "Weight")
```

each bee assessed three times

```{r}
summarySE(bee_data, groupvars = c("Tx"), measurevar = "Weight")
```

17 control, 21 in each duration x submersion treatment

```{r}
summarySE(bee_data, groupvars = c("Tx", "Duration", "Time"), measurevar = "Weight")

```

A follow-up study submersion [@rondeau2024] experiment compared survival
under three different conditions.

-   **control** (no water)

-   **floating** in water

-   maintained **underwater** via a plunger

![Three treatments used in the study. From Rondeau and Raine
2026.](rsbl.2023.0609.f001.png){fig-alt="Three test tubes are shown. A bee is in each, and each has dirt on the bottom. One bee is on the dirt (control), one is floating in water that has been added to the tube, and one is submerged in water by a plunger that has been used to cap the tube."}

Bees were initially placed in soil filled tubes and refrigerated. After
7 days, submersion treatments were applied. For the treatments with
water, bees were maintained for 8 hours, 24 hours, or 7 days. A total of
143 bees (17 control, 21 in each duration x treatment condition) were
used. After the experiment, all bees were returned to new tubes with
soil, returned to the refrigerator, then assessed for survival at one,
four, and eight weeks following the beginning of submersion treatments.

For our exam, we will focus on the data collected at eight weeks
following 24 hour submersion treatments. Below code creates a table if
you wish to use the combined data. Note the following columns are used

-   Submersion

    -   treatment (control; floating, underwater =submerged)

-   Weight

    -   weight in mg (measured before the study)

-   Survival

    -   1= survived; 0 = did not survive

```{r}
bee_data <- read.csv("data_flooding.csv", stringsAsFactors = T)
library(plyr)
bee_data$Submersion <-revalue(bee_data$Submersion, c("ctl"="control")) 
bee_data <- bee_data[bee_data$Time==8 & bee_data$Duration==24 & bee_data$Weight != "NA"|
                       bee_data$Time==8 & bee_data$Submersion=="control" & bee_data$Weight != "NA",]
bee_table <- table(bee_data[bee_data$Time==8 & bee_data$Duration==24|
                       bee_data$Time==8 & bee_data$Submersion=="control","Submersion"],
      bee_data[bee_data$Time==8 & bee_data$Duration==24|
                       bee_data$Time==8 & bee_data$Submersion=="control","Survival"])
colnames(bee_table) <- c("Survived", "Did not survive")
bee_table
```

Analyze the data. Make sure you include

-   null hypothesis (1 point)

-   alternative hypothesis (1 point)

-   explanation for test you will use (1.5 point)

-   results from statistical test (1 point)

    ```{r}
    chisq.test(bee_table)
    ```

    ```{r}
    chisq.test(bee_table)$expected
    ```

    ```{r}
    fisher.test(bee_table)
    ```

-   clear explanation of how results relate to your stated hypotheses
    (1.5 point)

## 5

Data was also collected on the weights of the bees (*Weight* column in
**bee_data**). Plot the weight data to consider differences among
submersion treatments.

```{r}
library(Rmisc)
library(ggplot2)
bee_summary <- summarySE(bee_data, measurevar="Weight", groupvars="Submersion")
ggplot(bee_summary, aes(x=Submersion, y=Weight)) +
    geom_point(size=3) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=Weight - ci, ymax=Weight + ci), width=0) +
    ylab("Mass (mg)") +
    xlab("Treatment") +
    ggtitle("Mass by submersion treatment")
```

```{r}
ggplot(bee_data, aes(y=Weight, x=Submersion, color=Submersion)) +
  geom_jitter() +
  labs(title="Masses of bees used in various treaments",
       subtitle = "There is no apparent difference in weights",
       y= "Bee weight (mg)",
       x= "Treatment")+
  guides(color=F)
```

## 6

study differed from typical queen weights. A typical queen at the stage
used in the study weighs 450 mg.

Investigate the question. Make sure you include

-   explanation for test you will use (1.5 point)

